source: Harrell (2011) Argument diagramming and critical thinking in introductory philosophy (copy of the paper, first 100k of 142k characters read)
finding: Two naturalistic quasi-experiments (not randomised) in an intro philosophy course. Taught-diagramming sections beat untaught sections on the post-test, but the overall pre-to-post gain difference was not significant in either study.
numbers: Study 1 (Spring 2004): 35 taught vs 104 not taught; mean score pre 0.64/0.58, post 0.87/0.76, gain 0.22 vs 0.18; gain difference t(53)=1.35 p>.05; post-test ANCOVA F(1,133)=21.1 p<.001. Study 2 (Fall 2004): 68 vs 62; pre 0.48/0.44, post 0.70/0.62, gain 0.22 vs 0.18; gain difference t(126)=1.22 p>.05; post-test ANCOVA F(1,123)=5.92 p=.01. Total N=269.
limits: Own non-standard argument-analysis test, not the CCTST. Pre and post tests not known to be equivalent (author says the post-test may be easier). Taught group differed on pre-test in Study 1 (t(61)=2.50 p=.015). One lecturer for the Study 1 treatment group.
agent_relevance: Even in the favourable study the gain over control is 0.04 points on a 0-1 scale. A map step needs a control with equal practice time before any agent claim.

source: Harrell (2011), results split by pre-test level (same copy as d01)
finding: The benefit is concentrated in low pre-test students, but only in some cells. Low students gained more with diagramming in both studies; intermediate students gained more in Study 1 only; high students gained little either way.
numbers: Gain taught vs not taught. Study 1: low 0.40 vs 0.28 (n=6 vs 32; Tukey gain t(7)=2.48 p=.14, n.s.), intermediate 0.30 vs 0.18 (n=13 vs 47; t(32)=3.51 p<.01), high 0.10 vs 0.07 (n=16 vs 25). Study 2: low 0.39 vs 0.24 (n=24 vs 22; t(38)=3.57 p=.007), intermediate 0.17 vs 0.18 (n=21 vs 27), high 0.10 vs 0.09 (n=23 vs 13).
limits: Levels are tertiles of the pre-test, so regression to the mean can inflate low-group gains in both arms. The paper text calls the Study 1 low-group gain significant while its own p is .14. The intermediate benefit did not replicate in Study 2. No d=1.1 for low students appears in the text I read; the printed d values are within-group pre-post (Study 2 low: taught 3.3, not taught 1.7).
agent_relevance: Supports a gate (use mapping where the plain attempt is weak) as a hypothesis only. The earlier note of d=1.1 for Harrell low students should be dropped.

source: Harrell (2011), stated flaws and internal inconsistencies (same copy as d01)
finding: The paper has internal numeric mismatches and the author lists method flaws herself.
numbers: Text effect sizes for Study 1 intermediate (6.9 taught; 2.8 and 3.5 not taught) do not match Table 3 (6.1 and 2.4). Study 2 gain ANOVA quotes df 133 where the other Study 2 tests use 124.
limits: Read through a secondary copy; the final 42k characters (discussion) were not read.
agent_relevance: Treat Harrell effect sizes as rough. Cite the raw gains (0.22 vs 0.18) instead of the d values.

source: Harrell (2008) No computer program required: pencil-and-paper argument mapping, Teaching Philosophy
finding: Full text could not be obtained: philpapers, philarchive and kilthub returned a bot challenge or 403 for curl and WebFetch.
numbers: No numbers obtained. The 180-student figure in b14 is still unverified.
limits: Not read. Gap 9 stays open for the 2008 paper.

source: Nesbit and Liu (2025) Argument Mapping in Higher Education: A Systematic Review, Higher Education Quarterly (abstract via Crossref)
finding: The abstract says one goal was to assess the prospects for meta-analysis, and reports no pooled effect. It lists counts only.
numbers: 124 studies coded, 102 empirical; 44% on attitudes, 40% on collaborative mapping, 51% on quality or structure of maps. The effect of mapping on critical thinking was the most often investigated causal question.
limits: Abstract only; publisher page returned 403. The number of randomised or controlled studies is not in the abstract.
agent_relevance: Even the review's own aim shows pooling is not yet clean. Do not quote a pooled effect from it.

source: Davies and Calma (2026) Argument mapping improves critical thinking skills, chapter in Routledge International Handbook of Learning and Instruction in University Education, pp 209-225 (Crossref record)
finding: Crossref gives authors and pages but no abstract. Davies is a developer of the Reason! and Rationale tradition, so this is not an independent pooled estimate.
numbers: No pooled g or d obtained. The publisher page returned only the title.
limits: Metadata only. The earlier note (86 documents, large pooled effect) rests on a snippet and could not be re-checked; the search budget was exhausted.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open. Keep the lower 0.5 SD figure.

source: Frontiers in Psychology (2022) quasi-experiment on digital concept mapping for argumentation, doi 10.3389/fpsyg.2022.882370
finding: Intact classes, not randomised. A concept-mapping group beat a reading-and-questions control, but this is concept mapping to support argumentation, not argument mapping, and the control is passive.
numbers: Research group 96, control 131 (pre-test respondents 59 and 63). Mean total score 4.6 vs 3.4 out of 6; t(223)=5.80 p<.001; MANOVA F(3,221)=10.35 partial eta2 .123; factual .045, conceptual .083, procedural .092.
limits: Only the first 100k of 157k characters read. df 223 does not match 96+131. Not a standardised critical thinking test. Not argument mapping.
agent_relevance: Not usable as evidence for argument mapping. It shows that no randomised, actively controlled argument-mapping trial turned up in this pass either.

source: Search-result summary of a controlled trial with 81 undergraduate psychology students (Dwyer and colleagues, University of Galway repository)
finding: The snippet says mapping students beat controls on evaluation and inductive reasoning but did not differ from a hierarchical-summary group.
numbers: N=81 only. No effect sizes or assignment method seen. Page returned 403.
limits: Seen only in a search snippet. Matches the Dwyer pattern already in K07.
agent_relevance: Consistent with the view that any structured note-taking gives a similar gain.

source: Miandoab and Sarathy (2024) Let's Argue Both Sides: Argument Generation Can Force Small Models to Utilize Previously Inaccessible Reasoning Capabilities, arXiv 2410.12997
finding: The model writes arguments for and against each option, ranks them with a ranking step, then answers. Versus zero-shot chain of thought the gain is real on average for small and medium models and near zero for large ones. It is strongly task- and model-dependent.
numbers: Nine tasks, ten models (Gemma 2B/7B, Llama3 8B/70B, Phi3 3.8B, Mistral 7B, GPT-4o-mini, Qwen2 1.5B, Aya 35B). Mean gain of Argument Generation over CoT: 3.18% small models, 2.72% medium, 0.95% large. Table 2: where AG beats zero-shot CoT the best gain is 25.95% (Gemma 2B) and 23.15% (Llama3 8B). Phi3 3.8B gains only 4.62%. Absolute gap between the two AG variants 4.09% (Spearman 0.8351).
limits: Pro/con argument generation, not a full map with objections and rebuttals. An equal-token control was not found in the text I read; the method makes several calls. Table 1 columns are garbled in the PDF extraction so single cells were not cited. CoT wins on several tasks.
agent_relevance: Closest existing test of the K02 idea. It supports a gated, small-model use and warns that strong models gain almost nothing.

source: Critical-Questions-of-Thought: Steering LLM reasoning with Argumentative Querying, arXiv 2412.15177
finding: A Toulmin-based loop of eight critical questions the plan must pass (at least 7/8, relaxed to 5/8 after five rounds, ten rounds max) before the model answers. Judge scores beat the standard output and zero-shot CoT in most cells.
numbers: MT-Bench Reasoning and Math, 40 questions per model, GPT-4o judge 1-10. Reasoning standard/CoT/CQoT: Claude Sonnet 3.5 8.6/8.55/8.95; GPT-4o 8.3/8.2/8.45; Gemini 1.5 Pro 8.45/8.25/8.9; Llama 3.1 70B 8.05/7.5/8.4; Nemotron 51B 6.75/7.7/7.3 (CoT won). Math, Llama: 8.95/9.35/9.55. CQoT best in 18 of 20 cells. Reported average gains 4.61% and 5.4% (their Table 3 gives slightly different averages).
limits: Tiny sample, no significance tests, LLM judge with length bias, possible MT-Bench contamination, and many extra calls so compute is not matched. It is a checking loop, not a map.
agent_relevance: Evidence that structured questioning (an S5-like critique) can help more than free CoT, but cost is higher. Do not credit it to the diagram form.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet, ICLR 2024, arXiv 2310.01798 (intrinsic self-correction table)
finding: Asking a model to critique and revise its own reasoning with no outside signal does not help and often hurts.
numbers: GPT-3.5: GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 to 74.7 over two rounds; CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0 to 25.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 79.5 to 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 to 49.0 to 43.0. GSM8K with GPT-3.5: the model keeps its first answer 74.7% of the time and turns right answers wrong more often than wrong to right.
limits: Prompts follow the source papers; answers are short. Not about maps.
agent_relevance: Supports the idea that a map revision must be driven by a located failure (code check or test), not by self-critique. Gap 7: indirect support, not a direct test.

source: Huang et al. (2024), oracle-label rows of the same paper
finding: When the revision step is told whether the answer is right, accuracy jumps. This isolates the value of a trusted failure signal.
numbers: Oracle self-correction: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 84.3, CommonSenseQA 89.7, HotpotQA 29.0 (standard 75.9/75.8/26.0). GPT-4: 97.5/85.5/59.0 (standard 95.5/82.0/49.0).
limits: Oracle labels are not available in real use; they show an upper bound. Table columns were read from a text extraction with misaligned rows.
agent_relevance: G2 and G4: where we have a checker (code, tests), revision on a located failure is the useful loop; a map alone adds nothing.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning, arXiv 2203.11171
finding: Sampling many reasoning paths and taking the majority answer lifts accuracy, and low agreement among samples indicates low confidence.
numbers: Gains over CoT: GSM8K +17.9, SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2 (code-davinci-002 GSM8K 78.0). The paper says low consistency can serve as an indicator of low model confidence.
limits: Costs many samples. The gap-6 comparison with graph features of a single trace is only in Baur et al. (earlier evidence), where sample consistency won for one model.
agent_relevance: Baseline for an S7 selection hint: sample agreement is cheap and code-computed. Graph features must beat it to be worth adding.

source: Dejl, Williams and Toni (2026) Argumentation for Explainable and Globally Contestable Decision Support with LLMs (ArgEval), arXiv 2603.14643
finding: Building one general argument framework per decision option once, then scoring cases against it, roughly matches base LLM and per-case ArgLLM accuracy at far lower token cost, but results swing with hyperparameters. The graph is code-aggregated (DF-QuAD) and editable.
numbers: Glioblastoma treatment ranking, 9 options. gpt-oss-20b: base LLM label-match 0.8775, NDCG 0.9578, 16.95M/6.59M tokens; ArgLLMs-O 0.8614 to 0.8444, NDCG 0.9739 to 0.9707, about 80-96M/20-23M tokens; ArgEval 0.4432 to 0.8485 across variants, about 1.2M/0.7M tokens at depth 1. Qwen3-30B: base 0.8630, NDCG 0.9527; best ArgEval 0.8818, NDCG 0.9771 (depth 2, 2.31M/1.38M tokens). Depth-2 ArgEval used 2.4x fewer completion tokens than the cheapest base run.
limits: One medical domain, expert-built labels, one run per variant. Root-score-estimation variants did poorly. Patient data enters only at the inference stage.
agent_relevance: The one recent system here that uses a code-validated argument graph in a decision loop with a measured cost win. The benefit is cost and contestability, not accuracy over the base model.

source: Henselmans, Prinzhorn and Libert (2026) Measuring AI Accountability Through Argumentation Analysis, arXiv 2609.05088
finding: Nine frontier models defended verdicts against critical questions, scored on Govier cogency. A model's stated justification scheme differs from the one it reasoned with on about a fifth of dilemmas.
numbers: 200 MoralChoice items, 6,778 judge-scored cells, 89.6% inter-judge agreement on 3,389 paired cells. Failure in 18.2% of cells; two outliers (Claude Sonnet 4.6, Llama 3.3) hold 67.8% of failures; Claude Sonnet 4.6 failure 54.8%. Reasoning-track and justification-track schemes differ in about 20% per model.
limits: Moral dilemmas, LLM judges, no accuracy outcome.
agent_relevance: A map written after the answer is a post-hoc justification and may not match the reasoning used. Build the map before the answer and check it against the final choice.

source: arXiv search pages for 'argument map' LLM and 'argument mapping language model reasoning' (checked 2026-11-19)
finding: The exact-phrase search returned one hit (Graphionale) and the looser query 14. None is a map-first versus chain-of-thought test at equal tokens, and none tests a deployed Rationale, Carneades or Argdown loop with a measured benefit.
numbers: Exact phrase: 1 result (2608.27932). Looser query: 14 results (2025-2026) including ARBITRA 2610.39433, Toulmin alignment 2608.29529, argument mining 2605.13793, ArgEval 2603.14643, DeceptionAnalyser 2609.24369.
limits: Keyword index only; papers that say 'argument graph' or 'dialectical' may be missed. Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and the arXiv API were rate limited and the WebSearch budget ran out.
agent_relevance: Absence evidence for K18. The direct experiment still has to be run.

source: DeceptionAnalyser (2026) web tool for structured deception analysis with argumentation schemes and LLMs, arXiv 2609.24369
finding: Only the title and the first line of the abstract were seen. It is a tool that applies argument schemes with LLMs to analysts' work.
agent_relevance: Possible lead for gap 10 (tools in loops); no measured benefit known.
